digest.top_line: PE-PE: adding 1y perioperative pembrolizumab to SABR/surgery MDT in omRCC gave mRFS 25.4 vs 11.0mo, HR 0.47 (0.24-0.92), randomized phase II.
digest.tldr: Organ preservation carried GI: AZUR-1 dostarlimab alone in dMMR/MSI-H LARC gave cCR12 68% (INV), single-arm interim; SANO surveillance after cCR to nCRT gave 5y OS 50% vs 54% but distant mets 46% vs 29%. PE-PE added pembrolizumab to MDT in omRCC (mRFS HR 0.47); PAM50 luminal-B predicted STADT benefit in RTOG 0534.

sites.intro: Post-RP salvage RT biomarkers: Decipher prognostic in 9601, PAM50 luminal-B a candidate predictor of STADT benefit.

studies.name: Decipher and PAM50 in NRG/RTOG 9601 and 0534
studies.tldr: ASTRO 2026 secondary analyses: Decipher prognostic in 9601 but not formally predictive; PAM50 luminal-B predicted STADT benefit with salvage RT in 0534.
details: 🔍 UroToday interview covering two ASTRO 2026 biomarker abstracts in post-RP salvage RT
🔍 RTOG 9601: salvage RT ± bicalutamide 24 mo, PSA 0.2 to 4.0, early and late salvage
🔗 9601 parent result: 7% absolute OS benefit at 15 yr with bicalutamide

subdetails: Prognostic for OS, PCSM and DM beyond clinical variables
Prognostic in the early salvage subgroup as well as the whole cohort
Did not meet the statistical criterion for a predictive biomarker

details.text: 📊 9601 decision tree: 15-yr PCSM benefit from bicalutamide, by PSA then Decipher

details: ⚠️ PSA cut defining early vs late salvage not stated in source
📐 Decipher 0.6 cut = dataset median; best-fit cut in early salvage was 0.61
🔗 NRG GU-009/010 (intact setting) used Decipher 0.85; cut points not interchangeable across settings
🔍 RTOG 0534: PBRT vs PBRT + STADT vs PBRT + STADT + PLNRT, biomarker subset only
📊 PAM50 in 0534: luminal-B gained large FFP benefit from STADT; non-luminal-B much less; interaction p significant (value not in source)
📊 MFS pattern similar, less pronounced; no effect size reported in source
🔗 Consistent with NRG-GU006 (apalutamide), where luminal-B also benefited from hormone therapy
⚠️ PLNRT trend by subtype on MFS called exploratory, not significant; not practice-changing per presenter
⚠️ Substudy far smaller than parent trial; presenter cautions against over-interpretation
studies.significance: The actionable split is early salvage with low Decipher: no significant 15-yr PCSM benefit from bicalutamide, while late salvage benefited regardless of score. PAM50 luminal-B status, reported on the Decipher grid, adds a predictive read for STADT. The PLNRT-by-subtype MFS trend is exploratory and should not yet move pelvic nodal coverage decisions.
studies.monday_clinic: In a post-RP pt with early salvage PSA and Decipher ≤0.6, this questions the PCSM value of adding hormone therapy to salvage RT; it does not extend to late salvage pts, who benefited regardless of score.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Two ASTRO 2026 **secondary biomarker analyses** of randomized salvage trials, discussed in a UroToday interview. **RTOG 9601**: salvage RT ± bicalutamide 24 mo. **RTOG 0534**: PBRT vs PBRT + STADT vs PBRT + STADT + PLNRT, PAM50 on a subset.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Post-prostatectomy salvage pts. 9601 enrolled **PSA 0.2 to 4.0**, early and late salvage. The 0534 PAM50 subset showed no significant baseline differences across arms.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Decipher was **prognostic** for OS, PCSM and DM, including early salvage, but **not predictive** by the statistical criterion. In 0534, luminal-B pts gained a **large FFP benefit from STADT** vs much less in non-luminal-B, with a significant interaction p.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The PAM50 finding matches **NRG-GU006**, where luminal-B tumors benefited from apalutamide, so the signal holds across bicalutamide, leuprolide-based STADT and an ARPI. NRG GU-009/010 used a Decipher cut of **0.85** in the intact setting, vs **0.6** here post-op.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents post-prostatectomy pts receiving salvage prostate bed RT with a decision about adding hormone therapy. Does not represent the intact-prostate definitive setting or the decision about pelvic nodal RT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: No HRs, interaction p-values or absolute rates are given in the source interview. The PSA threshold separating early from late salvage is not stated. Decipher and PAM50 can be **discordant**, and the source offers no data on how to resolve that.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Presenters frame both tests as one input to **shared decision-making** with pts, not a gate. Decipher reports PAM50 subtype on the same grid, so a single order yields both.

studies.interpretation:
The two abstracts answer different questions, and it helps to keep them apart. Decipher in RTOG 9601 is a risk discriminator: it sorts pts by how likely they are to metastasize or die of prostate cancer, with treatment-adjusted models that hold in the early salvage subgroup most US pts now fall into. What it did not do is clear the bar for prediction, meaning the relative benefit of bicalutamide did not differ by score in a statistically convincing way. The decision tree, which finds no significant PCSM benefit only in early salvage with low Decipher, is therefore an absolute-risk argument. Low-risk pts have little to gain in absolute terms, even if the relative effect is constant. That is a legitimate basis for de-intensification, but it is a different claim from saying the drug does not work in that group.

PAM50 makes the stronger mechanistic claim. In the 0534 subset, the luminal-B versus non-luminal-B interaction for STADT benefit on FFP was significant, and the direction matches NRG-GU006 with apalutamide and earlier retrospective cohorts. Agreement across three hormone strategies is the most persuasive part of the story, because it argues the subtype is reading androgen dependence rather than the behavior of one agent. The caveat is sample: only part of 0534 had evaluable tissue, and the presenter repeatedly cautioned that most p-values were modest and the endpoints imperfect.

For the RT reader, the PLNRT observation is the tempting one and the least supported. An MFS trend by subtype between the nodal and no-nodal arms, absent on FFP and not significant, is a hypothesis for a future trial, not a field-size criterion. Nothing here should change who gets pelvic nodes.

Two practical gaps stand out. The cut points do not transfer: 0.6 was the 9601 dataset median, while GU-009/010 used 0.85 in intact disease, so a single universal Decipher threshold does not exist. And discordance between a high Decipher score and a non-luminal-B call is acknowledged without data on how to resolve it. Without published effect sizes, interaction p-values or the PSA cut separating early from late salvage, the reasonable read is that these tools refine counseling in salvage RT and point toward subtype-directed trials. They do not yet replace PSA and clinical risk as the backbone of the ADT decision.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: For salvage prostate bed RT, low-Decipher early salvage pts showed no significant PCSM gain from adding bicalutamide, while late salvage benefited regardless. A PAM50 luminal-B trend toward PLNRT benefit on MFS appeared in 0534 but is exploratory and does not support changing nodal fields.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: PAM50 luminal-B predicted benefit from STADT in 0534 (significant interaction), matching NRG-GU006 with apalutamide, which suggests the effect does not depend on the agent. Decipher stayed prognostic but did not meet the predictive criterion, so it refines absolute risk rather than identifying who responds to ADT.

open_questions: Does PAM50 luminal-B status predict benefit from pelvic nodal RT?
How to act on discordant Decipher and PAM50 results
Optimal Decipher cut point for de-intensifying ADT in early salvage

sites.intro: dMMR/MSI-H LARC moving toward PD-1 blockade alone, with RT and surgery omitted in responders.

studies.name: AZUR-1
studies.tldr: cCR12 68% (investigator) and cCR12+pCR 76% with dostarlimab alone in dMMR/MSI-H LARC, no recurrences to date at 26.3mo median f/u.
details: 🔍 Global single-arm phase II, registrational; interim analysis, N=154 enrolled, DCO 20 April 2026
💊 Dostarlimab 500 mg IV q3w × 9 cycles, no chemo, RT or planned surgery
🔍 Median f/u 26.3mo (range 2-36); 144 pts with ≥12mo f/u evaluable for cCR12 (INV)
📊 15 pts went to surgery after dostarlimab alone: 12 (80%) pCR → composite cCR12+pCR 76%
📊 98% of cCR pts held cCR ≥12mo; no recurrences to date after cCR or pCR
📊 93% in surveillance without progression (dostarlimab ± SOC); 71% with dostarlimab alone
📊 88% completed all 9 cycles; G≥3 immune-mediated AEs in 4 pts
🔗 Context: source cites post-TNT cCR range of 21-41% in unselected LARC
⚠️ ICR cCR12 47% vs INV 68%: different denominators, 38 pts still in cCR awaiting cCR12 at DCO
⚠️ Single-arm, no randomised comparator vs TNT or chemoRT; interim read with ongoing f/u

verdict.rationale: Single-arm interim analysis without a randomised comparator; investigator vs central review cCR12 diverge, and durability beyond 26.3mo median f/u is unproven.
verdict.audience: dMMR/MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer, treatment-naive

studies.significance: The RT-omission read hinges on the assessor: investigator cCR12 is 68%, central review 47% (54/116) with 38 pts still pending. Either figure exceeds the 21-41% post-TNT cCR range the source cites, which supports MMR testing before any pelvic RT is planned in LARC.
studies.monday_clinic: In dMMR/MSI-H LARC, this supports checkpoint-first, organ-preservation discussion before committing to chemoRT or TNT; it does not extend to pMMR/MSS rectal cancer.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Global **single-arm phase II**, registrational. **Interim analysis**, N=154 enrolled, median f/u **26.3 mo** (range 2-36).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **dMMR/MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer**. 144 pts had ≥12 mo f/u for investigator-assessed cCR12.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: **Dostarlimab 500 mg IV q3w for 9 cycles** as monotherapy; chemotherapy, radiation and surgery reserved for non-responders.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Key endpoints: **sustained cCR for 12 months (cCR12)** after end of treatment by investigator and independent central review, and composite cCR12 (INV) + pCR.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: cCR12 **68%** (INV) vs **47% (54/116)** (ICR); composite cCR12+pCR **76%**. Of 15 resected pts, 12 (80%) had pCR; **no recurrences** to date after cCR or pCR.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **88%** completed all 9 cycles. G≥3 immune-mediated AEs in **4 pts**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Post-TNT cCR is cited at **21-41%** in LARC broadly; AZUR-1 exceeds that in a biomarker-selected group. It scales up the earlier small dostarlimab study that first showed durable cCR in dMMR LARC.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents dMMR/MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer treated with PD-1 monotherapy first. Does not represent pMMR/MSS rectal cancer, where TNT and chemoRT remain the backbone.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Investigator and central review diverge on cCR12, and ICR evaluability lagged because cCR was confirmed later. cCR12 is a surrogate for durable organ preservation; local regrowth risk beyond 3 years is unmeasured.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Durable cCR with no recurrences so far makes **RT omission** a realistic default question in dMMR LARC. Open: how long surveillance must run, and what salvage looks like for late regrowth.

studies.interpretation:
AZUR-1 moves the dMMR/MSI-H rectal question from a single remarkable cohort to a multinational registrational dataset, and the central finding holds at scale: most pts given nine cycles of dostarlimab and nothing else are sitting in sustained clinical complete response at a median of 26.3 months. For a radiation oncologist, this is the most direct challenge yet to reflexive pelvic chemoRT or TNT in this biomarker group. The comparison the source draws, 21-41% cCR after TNT, is not a like-for-like benchmark because it comes from unselected LARC, but the gap is wide enough that selection alone does not plausibly explain it.

The methodological detail that should move confidence most is the split between investigator and central review. Investigator cCR12 is 68%; independent central review is 47% (54/116), with 38 pts still in cCR and awaiting the 12-month mark. The investigators attribute the gap to central reviewers confirming cCR later than the initial end-of-treatment assessment, which would shift pts into a pending bucket rather than into failure. That explanation is plausible and the 98% durability figure among responders supports it, but it is also exactly the pattern one would see if central readers were stricter about what counts as a complete response on endoscopy and MRI. Until the pending 38 resolve, the honest range for this endpoint sits between the two figures, and the registrational read will likely rest on the ICR number.

The pathology data are small but informative. Only 15 pts went to surgery after dostarlimab alone, and 12 of them had pCR. That tells us the clinical non-responders are not uniformly true non-responders, which raises the question of whether some resections in this setting were avoidable with longer observation, a timing issue the trial does not settle.

What the trial cannot answer is late behaviour. Watch-and-wait experience after chemoRT has taught the field that local regrowth can appear after the first two years, and the absence of recurrence to date is bounded by follow-up that ranges from 2 to 36 months. A single-arm design also leaves no estimate of what RT would add for the minority who do not reach cCR, or whether sequencing RT after incomplete response preserves the organ as often as upfront TNT would have.

Practically, the result reinforces two things: MMR status belongs at the start of LARC workup, before RT simulation, and in dMMR disease the RT decision is increasingly a salvage decision rather than a definitive one. What would make this wrong is a late regrowth signal, or central review cCR12 failing to recover toward the investigator figure as the pending pts mature.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Central review cCR12 is 47% (54/116) against investigator 68%, with 38 pts pending; both exceed the 21-41% post-TNT cCR range cited. In dMMR/MSI-H LARC, pelvic RT is shifting toward a salvage role, so MMR status should be known before simulation.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Nine cycles of dostarlimab 500 mg q3w delivered 68% cCR12 (INV) with 88% completing therapy and G≥3 immune-mediated AEs in 4 pts. This positions PD-1 monotherapy as the first move in dMMR/MSI-H LARC, ahead of oxaliplatin-based TNT.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Only 15 pts underwent resection after dostarlimab alone and 12 (80%) were pCR, so most surgical specimens showed no residual tumour. The surgical question becomes timing of salvage and surveillance intervals, not upfront TME, in dMMR/MSI-H LARC.

open_questions: Will ICR cCR12 converge with investigator rate as pending pts mature?
Late local regrowth risk beyond 3 years without RT or surgery
Role of RT for dMMR pts without cCR after dostarlimab

sites.intro: Surveillance after cCR to nCRT spares oesophagectomy at the cost of a distant mets excess.

studies.name: SANO
studies.tldr: 5y OS 50% vs 54%, HR 1.17 (0.77-1.77) active surveillance vs surgery after cCR to nCRT; distant mets 46% vs 29%, P<.01.

details.text: 📊 5y outcomes, active surveillance vs standard surgery

details: 🔍 Multicentre stepped-wedge cluster-randomised non-inferiority trial, 2017-2021, N=309
🔍 cCR = no tumour on endoscopic biopsies, endoscopic ultrasound, or PET-CT after nCRT
📐 Median f/u 76 mo (IQR 67-86); OS similar across histologic subtypes (no subgroup HRs in source)
📊 85/198 (43%) spared non-beneficial oesophagectomy
⚠️ The 'spared' count includes pts with distant mets detected within 6 mo of nCRT, so it is not purely organ preservation
⚠️ OS CI upper bound 1.77; 'not significantly different' at 5y is not non-inferiority, and no 5y NI margin is reported
⚠️ Distant mets excess under surveillance is unexplained in source: delayed salvage vs detection timing
⚠️ Cluster-level stepped-wedge allocation with unequal arms (198 vs 111); nCRT regimen and RT dose not stated in source

verdict.rationale: Long-term f/u of a cluster-randomised NI trial supporting emerging organ preservation; wide OS CI and a significant distant-mets excess stop short of practice-changing.
verdict.audience: Locally advanced oesophageal cancer, cCR after nCRT

studies.significance: The RT read is that nCRT alone was the definitive treatment for 43% of the surveillance arm, but distant mets rose to 46% vs 29% without immediate surgery. That makes cCR after nCRT a reasonable organ-preservation endpoint for selected pts. Whether early oesophagectomy suppresses distant spread, or the gap comes from how surveillance detects disease, is the open question.
studies.monday_clinic: In locally advanced oesophageal cancer with cCR on biopsies, EUS and PET-CT after nCRT, this supports active surveillance with surgery as needed as a discussable option; it does not address pts without cCR or nCRT regimens other than those used in SANO.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Multicentre **stepped-wedge cluster-randomised non-inferiority** trial, 2017-2021, Netherlands Trial Register NTR-6803. This report covers **5y outcomes** at median f/u 76 mo (IQR 67-86).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Locally advanced oesophageal cancer** with a **complete clinical response after nCRT**, defined as no tumour on endoscopic biopsies, endoscopic ultrasound, or PET-CT. N=309: 198 active surveillance, 111 standard surgery.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: nCRT was the common backbone. The regimen, dose and fractionation are **not stated in source**, so whether the result transfers to a given chemoRT protocol cannot be judged from this abstract.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: The earlier report showed non-inferiority on **two-year OS** with improved QoL under surveillance. This analysis compares 5y OS and DFS by Cox regression and estimates distant metastasis incidence with competing-risk analysis.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: OS and DFS were **not significantly different**, but **distant mets were higher under surveillance (P<.01)**. **85/198 (43%)** were spared non-beneficial oesophagectomy.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: This extends SANO's own 2y non-inferiority result and follows the preSANO cCR-assessment framework. It parallels the watch-and-wait paradigm in rectal cancer (OPRA). The randomised definitive-CRT question is being tested separately in NEEDS.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents locally advanced oesophageal cancer with cCR on biopsies, EUS and PET-CT after nCRT. Does not represent pts with residual disease after nCRT or those not fit for salvage oesophagectomy.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The 43% spared figure counts pts with **distant mets within 6 mo of nCRT**, which inflates the organ-preservation benefit. At 5y, no NI margin is reported, and an OS HR upper bound of 1.77 cannot exclude clinically relevant harm.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Survival parity holds at 5y, but the distant-mets excess is the signal to explain. It could reflect micrometastatic seeding during delayed resection, or disease surfacing on surveillance imaging that resection would have found later. The abstract cannot separate the two.

studies.interpretation:
The five-year SANO data shift the debate on organ preservation in oesophageal cancer. The question is no longer whether active surveillance is safe in the short term. It is what kind of failure surveillance trades for avoiding surgery. Overall survival stays close between strategies (HR 1.17, 95% CI 0.77-1.77) after a median 76 months, and DFS points the same way without reaching significance (HR 1.39, 0.94-2.06). Taken alone, those numbers suggest the 2-year non-inferiority result held. The finding that complicates that reading is the cumulative incidence of distant metastases: 46% under surveillance vs 29% after standard surgery, P<.01.

There are two broad explanations, and they lead to different practice. The first is biological: residual microscopic disease that biopsies, EUS and PET-CT missed keeps seeding while the primary is watched, and an early oesophagectomy removes that source. If so, the survival parity may wear down with longer follow-up, or may be held up only by effective salvage of locoregional regrowth. The second is about how failure is counted. Under surveillance, distant disease may be picked up and recorded where, after resection, it would have shown up at a later restaging. The fact that OS has not diverged argues somewhat for the second explanation, but the abstract cannot settle it. A reader should treat the metastasis signal as unresolved, not as noise.

The design deserves attention. A stepped-wedge cluster-randomised trial allocates centres to the timing of a strategy switch, not individual patients to an arm. That explains the unequal groups (198 vs 111) and makes the comparison more exposed to calendar-time and centre effects than an individually randomised trial. The non-inferiority framing also does less work at five years than at two. The source reports no 5-year margin, and an upper confidence bound of 1.77 is wide enough to include a harm most clinicians would reject. "Not statistically significantly different" is the right description. Equivalence is not.

The 43% figure (85/198 spared non-beneficial oesophagectomy) needs careful reading. It includes patients whose distant metastases appeared within six months of nCRT, for whom avoiding surgery reflects early systemic failure rather than successful organ preservation. Those patients gain something real, because a futile oesophagectomy is avoided. But the number of patients with a durable, sustained cCR is smaller than 43%, and the abstract does not give it on its own.

For a radiation oncologist, SANO makes nCRT a potentially definitive treatment for responders, so cCR assessment becomes the gate that decides the management path. It raises two questions the abstract cannot answer. First, would a different nCRT dose or schedule raise the durable cCR fraction, given that the regimen is not stated here? Second, should the distant-mets excess prompt systemic intensification during surveillance? Ongoing randomised work on definitive chemoradiation with salvage surgery, such as NEEDS, is better placed to answer the dose question than SANO is.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: nCRT alone was definitive treatment for a large part of the surveillance arm, which makes cCR on biopsies, EUS and PET-CT the decision gate. The nCRT regimen is not stated in source, so dose transfer cannot be judged, and the distant-mets excess (46% vs 29%) matters when counselling responders.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Surgery as needed spared 85/198 (43%) a non-beneficial oesophagectomy with no significant 5y OS difference (HR 1.17). The distant-mets excess under surveillance (P<.01) raises the question of whether delaying resection gives up systemic control, and that 43% includes pts who progressed within 6 mo.

open_questions: Why are distant metastases higher under active surveillance?
Does systemic therapy during surveillance offset the distant-mets excess?
Which nCRT regimen maximizes durable cCR?

sites.intro: Randomized phase II signal that IO adds RFS to SABR-dominant MDT in oligometastatic RCC.

studies.name: PE-PE
studies.tldr: mRFS 25.4 vs 11.0 mo, HR 0.47 (0.24-0.92), p=0.024, adding 1y perioperative pembrolizumab to SABR/surgery MDT in omRCC.

details.text: 📊 P+MDT vs MDT alone, median f/u 17.5 mo

details: 🔍 Randomized 2:1, open-label, multicenter phase II, N=85 (March 2023 to February 2026)
🔍 Prior nephrectomy, ≤3 mets within 5y of Nx or prior metastasectomy
💊 Pembrolizumab 400 mg q6w × 9 cycles (1y); first dose given before MDT
🔍 MDT modality balanced: SABR 73% vs 72%, surgery 23% vs 28%
⚠️ SABR dose/fractionation not reported in source
⚠️ Local relapse and distant RFS were secondary endpoints, not reported in source
⚠️ Only 2 deaths (one per arm); OS uninformative at this f/u
⚠️ Median 6.6 of 9 planned cycles; discontinuation for PD in 11, AE in 4

subdetails: Two pts G3, no G4 or G5

details: 🔗 Extends the adjuvant pembrolizumab M1NED rationale (KEYNOTE-564) to unresected oligomets treated with MDT

verdict.rationale: Randomized phase II met its RFS primary, but N=85 with a 29-pt control arm, 17.5-mo median f/u, open-label, and only 2 deaths; abstract-only.
verdict.audience: Oligometastatic RCC, ≤3 mets within 5y of prior nephrectomy, MDT-eligible

studies.significance: SABR was the MDT in 73% vs 72% of pts, so this is mostly pembrolizumab plus SABR vs SABR alone. Dose/fractionation and the local relapse secondary aren't in the abstract, so it can't yet show whether P changes in-field control or only cuts distant events. The decision it moves is whether SABR to all sites goes ahead with or without IO.
studies.monday_clinic: In post-nephrectomy omRCC with ≤3 mets within 5y planned for SABR or metastasectomy, this supports discussing 1y of perioperative pembrolizumab with MDT; it does not extend to >3 mets or relapse beyond 5y of nephrectomy.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Randomized **2:1**, open-label, multicenter **phase II**, **N=85** (56 P+MDT, 29 MDT alone). Median follow-up **17.5 mo**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: omRCC after **prior nephrectomy**, **≤3 metastases** within **5 years** of Nx or prior metastasectomy, candidates for MDT to all metastatic sites. Baseline characteristics reported as balanced.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Pembrolizumab **400 mg q6w × 9 cycles (1 year)**, first dose **before MDT**. Median cycles delivered **6.6**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: MDT was **SABR in 73% vs 72%** and surgery in 23% vs 28%. **Dose, fractionation and target definition not reported in source.**

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: relapse-free survival.** Secondary: distant RFS, local relapse, OS, safety; only safety secondaries are reported in the abstract.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Any AE **80% vs 21%**, G3 **7% vs 3%**. P-related AEs 59%, led by hypothyroidism 23%; no G4/5.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: KEYNOTE-564 established adjuvant pembrolizumab after Nx and for M1NED within 1 year of Nx. PE-PE moves that into **unresected oligomets ablated by SABR or surgery**, including relapse up to 5 years out.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents post-nephrectomy omRCC with ≤3 metastases within 5 years, all sites treatable by SABR or surgery. Does not represent pts with >3 metastases, no prior nephrectomy, or relapse beyond 5 years.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: No local vs distant relapse split, so the **site of benefit is unknown**. RFS assessor blinding not stated in an open-label trial, and 2 of the 9 planned cycles went undelivered at the median.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The RFS gain is large but rests on 35 events, with a CI upper bound of 0.92. It **does not settle** whether IO at MDT beats IO deferred to relapse, which is the comparison that decides treatment-free intervals.

studies.interpretation:
The question PE-PE answers is narrower than its headline. Adjuvant pembrolizumab is already standard after nephrectomy for high-risk disease and for M1NED within a year of nephrectomy, the population KEYNOTE-564 defined. PE-PE carries that principle to pts whose metastases are still present but limited (≤3) and ablatable, and whose relapse may come up to 5 years after nephrectomy, well outside the 1-year M1NED window. Read that way, the result extends accepted biology rather than departing from it: anti-PD-1 given around the time all visible disease is eradicated delays relapse. The point estimate, HR 0.47 with mRFS 25.4 vs 11.0 mo, is large, but the upper CI bound of 0.92 shows how little information 35 events carry, and the true effect could plausibly be modest.

For a radiation oncologist the trial is functionally pembrolizumab plus SABR vs SABR alone, since SABR was the MDT in 73% vs 72% of pts. The abstract gives no dose, fractionation or target definition, and it withholds the two secondaries that would tell us where the benefit sits: local relapse and distant RFS. That split decides how the RT reader should use the result. If the gain is entirely at new distant sites, P is treating occult disease SABR never saw, SABR technique is unchanged, and the question is purely a systemic add-on. If in-field failure also drops, there is an interaction worth testing directly, and dose de-escalation or lesion selection questions open up. Until those endpoints are published, neither reading is supported.

Several design features should temper confidence. The trial is open-label, and the source does not say whether relapse was assessed centrally or blinded; imaging-defined RFS in an unblinded trial is sensitive to assessment timing. The 2:1 allocation leaves only 29 control pts, so the MDT-alone median of 11.0 mo rests on 16 events. Exposure was also below the nominal year, with a median of 6.6 of 9 cycles. On the toxicity side, any-grade AEs of 80% vs 21% and hypothyroidism in 23% are a permanent cost for pts who might have stayed relapse-free after MDT alone.

What the trial cannot answer is the comparison that matters most at the bedside: pembrolizumab with MDT vs MDT with IO deferred to relapse. An RFS gain without OS data, here 2 deaths in total, does not show that early IO beats IO at progression, and the MDT-alone pts will presumably receive systemic therapy when they relapse. For now this is a reason to discuss perioperative pembrolizumab with MDT-eligible pts and to watch for the local relapse and distant RFS data, not a settled standard.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: SABR was the MDT in 73% vs 72%, so this tests IO on top of SABR to all sites. Dose and the local relapse secondary are unreported, so whether P improves in-field control or only distant events is unknown, and SABR technique itself is unchanged.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: One year of pembrolizumab, started before MDT, gave HR 0.47 for RFS beyond the M1NED-within-1y adjuvant setting. G3 AEs were 7% and hypothyroidism 23%, and with 2 deaths there is no OS read to weigh against deferring IO until relapse.

OS benefit vs deferring IO until relapse after MDT

papers.title: PErioperative PEmbrolizumab (P) plus metastasis-directed therapy (MDT) versus MDT alone in patients (pts) with oligometastatic renal cell carcinoma (omRCC): The randomized phase II PE-PE trial
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract LBA88 · Proffered paper 2: Genitourinary tumours, renal and urothelial · 2026-10-25 · presented by Roberto Iacovelli (Rome, Italy) · NCT05578664

Background: Adjuvant P is the standard of care for pts with intermediate-high/high risk of relapse after nephrectomy (Nx), as well as for those with M1NED within 1y of previous Nx. Although omRCC pts may receive anti-PD-1-based combos, the optimal management of those eligible for MDT remains uncertain.
Methods: The PE-PE trial (NCT05578664) is a randomized, open-label, multicenter phase II study evaluating the efficacy of P in delaying tumor progression for omRCC pts candidates for MDT, including surgery or SABR to all metastatic sites. Eligible pts had undergone prior Nx and presented with ≤3 metastases within 5 years of Nx or previous metastasectomy. Pts were randomized 2:1 to receive P 400 mg every 6 weeks for 9 cycles (1 year) plus MDT (P+MDT) or MDT alone. The first dose of P was administered before MDT. The primary endpoint was relapse-free survival (RFS), while others included distant RFS, local relapse, OS, and safety.
Results: 85 pts were randomized between March 2023 and February 2026: 56 to the P+MDT arm and 29 to the MDT-alone arm. Baseline characteristics were well balanced between treatment groups. SABR was selected in 73% vs. 72% of pts, while surgery was performed in 23% vs. 28%, respectively. The median number of P cycles administered was 6.6. The most frequent reasons for P discontinuation were disease progression (11 pts) and adverse events (AE, 4 pts). After a median follow-up of 17.5 mos, 35 RFS events were observed (19 vs.16), with two deaths (one in each arm). Median RFS was 25.4 mos in the P+MDT arm vs. 11.0 mos in the MDT-alone arm (HR 0.47; 95% CI, 0.24-0.92; p=0.024). Regarding safety, 80% vs. 21% of pts experienced at least one AE, while G3 AEs occurred in 7% vs. 3% of pts in the P+MDT and MDT-alone arms, respectively. P-related AEs of any G occurred in 59%, the most common being hypothyroidism (23%), fatigue (18%), and diarrhea (16%). Two pts experienced G3 toxicity without G4 or 5.
Conclusions: The PE-PE trial supports the use of 1 year of perioperative P in pts with omRCC eligible for MDT, demonstrating a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in RFS with a manageable and consistent safety profile.
Clinical trial identification: NCT05578664.

papers.title: Clinical complete response with dostarlimab monotherapy in dMMR/MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC): First results from the global registrational AZUR-1 trial
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract LBA87 · Proffered paper: Gastrointestinal tumours, lower digestive · 2026-10-25 · presented by Andrea Cercek (New York, United States of America, NY) · NCT05723562

Background: Multimodal treatment with chemotherapy, radiation and surgery is a standard of care (SOC) for LARC associated with significant toxicity/morbidity. After TNT, the range of clinical complete response (cCR) is 21–41%. dMMR/MSI-H tumours are exceptionally responsive to PD-1 blockade: in a small study, neoadjuvant dostarlimab treatment led to durable cCRs and eliminated the need for SOC in most patients (pts) with LARC. AZUR-1 (NCT05723562) is a global single-arm trial and the first registrational study evaluating the clinical benefit of dostarlimab monotherapy in pts with dMMR/MSI-H LARC.
Methods: Dostarlimab 500 mg was administered IV every 3 weeks for 9 cycles. Key endpoints include rate of sustained cCR for 12 months (cCR12) following end of treatment (EOT) with dostarlimab alone by investigator (INV) and independent central review (ICR), and composite rate of cCR12 (INV) + pathological CR (pCR).
Results: At data cutoff (DCO, 20 April 2026), 154 pts were enrolled and median follow-up was 26.3 months (range 2–36). Of 144 pts with ≥12 months follow-up, 68% achieved cCR12 (INV). Of 15 pts who underwent surgery after dostarlimab alone, 12 (80%) had pCR, resulting in a cCR12+pCR rate of 76%. Fewer pts were cCR12-evaluable by ICR, primarily due to cCR being confirmed later by ICR after initial EOT evaluation. Of pts evaluable by ICR, 47% (54/116) achieved cCR12, with 38 pts in cCR and being followed for cCR12 at DCO. 98% of pts who achieved cCR remained in cCR for ≥12 months by INV or ICR, with no recurrences to date for pts who achieved cCR or pCR. Overall, 93% of patients are in surveillance with no evidence of disease progression after treatment (dostarlimab ± SOC) and 71% achieved this outcome with dostarlimab alone. The safety profile was acceptable: 88% of pts completed all 9 cycles of dostarlimab and Grade ≥3 immune-mediated AEs occurred in 4 pts.
Conclusions: In this AZUR-1 interim analysis, 68% of pts achieved cCR12 and 76% achieved cCR12+pCR with dostarlimab alone with no disease recurrences to date. These durable responses indicate the potential to eliminate the need for chemotherapy, radiation and surgery, and redefine the curative-intent treatment paradigm for pts with dMMR/MSI-H LARC.
Clinical trial identification: NCT05723562.

papers.title: Active surveillance versus standard surgery after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for oesophageal cancer: Long-term results of a cluster-randomised controlled trial (SANO)
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract LBA78 · Proffered paper 1: Gastrointestinal tumour, upper digestive · 2026-10-23 · presented by Sanjiv S. Gangaram-Panday (Rotterdam, Netherlands)

Background: The Surgery As Needed for Oesophageal cancer (SANO)-trial demonstrated that active surveillance is non-inferior to standard surgery in terms of two-year overall survival in patients with a complete clinical response after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (nCRT). Active surveillance resulted in improved quality of life. Here, we report 5-year outcomes.
Methods: From 2017 to 2021, a multicentre stepped-wedge cluster-randomised non-inferiority trial was conducted. Patients with locally advanced oesophageal cancer who achieved complete clinical response (defined as no tumour detected on endoscopic biopsies, -ultrasound, or PET-CT) underwent active surveillance or standard surgery. Cox regression was used to compare 5-year overall and disease-free survival, and the cumulative incidence of distant metastases was estimated using competing risk analysis.
Results: A total of 309 patients were included, 198 underwent active surveillance and 111 underwent standard surgery. Median follow-up was 76 months (IQR 67–86). Five-year overall survival was not statistically significantly different between active surveillance and standard surgery (50%, 95%CI 34-57 vs. 54%, 95%CI 46-64; HR 1.17, 95%CI 0.77-1.77) with similar results across histologic subtypes. Disease-free survival was not statistically significantly different (HR 1.39, 95% CI 0.94-2.06). The cumulative incidence of distant metastases at five years was significantly higher in the active surveillance group compared to the standard surgery group (46%, 95%CI 39-53 vs. 29%, 95%CI 21-37; P<.01). Overall, 85 of 198 patients (43%) were spared non-beneficial oesophagectomy, including those with sustained complete clinical response at last follow-up or distant metastases detected within six months after nCRT.
Conclusions: Overall survival at 5 years is not statistically significantly different between active surveillance and standard surgery in patients with oesophageal cancer and a complete clinical response after nCRT, despite a higher incidence of distant metastases in the active surveillance group. These findings support active surveillance as a feasible treatment strategy in these patients.
Clinical trial identification: The Netherlands Trial Register (NTR-6803).
